IANA's "IANA-managed Reserved Domains" page (https://www.iana.org/domains/reserved) explains that certain domains are set aside and nominally registered to "IANA" for specific policy or technical purposes:

2. Test IDN top-level domains: These were temporarily delegated by IANA for the IDN Evaluation conducted by ICANN. 3. Policy-reserved domains: IANA acts as both the registrant and registrar for a select number of domains reserved on policy grounds. These exclusions are typically indicated in technical standards (RFC documents) or contractual limitations. Domains described as registered to IANA or ICANN on policy grounds are not available for registration or transfer, with the exception of certain noted cases.

tasks.goal: Summarize IANA's role from its about page and cite the exact URL.

assertions.observed: IANA's role, per its about page (https://www.iana.org/about): IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) maintains the authoritative public registries that record allocations and definitions of the Internet's key technical identifiers so they mean the same thing everywhere — domain names and IP addresses must be assigned to a single party with the same global meaning, and protocol codes must be interpreted identically by all software. It provides a common global point of reference as a neutral, public-service steward: registries are openly published, services are free of charge, and it implements policies developed by the communities it serves. Its work includes processing identifier requests from standardization processes and users, assessing them against established policies, and operating the systems that publish the registries and their data, including infrastructure for producing, securing, and distributing key aspects of the DNS. These functions date back to the 1970s and are today performed by Public Technical Identifiers, a purpose-built affiliate of ICANN dedicated exclusively to delivering the IANA services. Source: https://www.iana.org/about

tasks.goal: Explain the role of Playwright locators and cite the exact API URL.

assertions.observed:
Playwright locators are "the central piece of Playwright's auto-waiting and retry-ability." In a nutshell, a locator represents a way to find element(s) on the page at any moment — unlike element handles, it re-resolves to elements at action time, enabling auto-waiting and retries. A locator is typically created with the page.locator() method (e.g., page.get_by_role('listitem')), and the Locator class provides methods such as all() (added in v1.29), which returns an array of locators when the locator points to a list of elements (note: locator.all() does not wait for elements to match and can be flaky with dynamically changing lists).

Exact API URL: https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api/class-locator (title: "Locator | Playwright Python").

tasks.goal: Starting from a blank page, use browser search to find an official GitHub Docs page that explains Git versus GitHub, explain the distinction, and cite the exact URL you used.

Exact URL used (confirmed via get_url on the live page): https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/start-your-journey/what-is-github

The distinction, as stated in the page's "GitHub and Git" section:
- Git is an open-source version control system that tracks changes to files. It lets you work on your own copy of a project, record a history of your changes, and merge your work with other people's changes safely.
- GitHub is a platform that builds on Git: it hosts your Git projects (called repositories) and supports your entire software development process across every stage of the software development life cycle — Plan (track work, set milestones, organize projects), Create (write and store code, develop features safely), Review (suggest changes, discuss with reviewers), Test (automate checks before merging), Deploy (automated deployment workflows and release management), and Operate (monitor apps, manage dependencies, find and fix security issues).

In short: Git is the underlying version control tool for tracking and merging changes; GitHub is the hosted platform built on top of Git that stores your repositories and adds collaboration, automation, and project-management capabilities.

tasks.goal: Summarize GitHub's authentication guidance and cite the exact Docs URL.

assertions.observed:
GitHub's Docs page "About authentication to GitHub" (https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/about-authentication-to-github) summarizes the platform's authentication guidance as follows:

Core guidance: To keep your account secure, you must authenticate before accessing certain resources on GitHub. Authentication means supplying or confirming credentials unique to you to prove you are exactly who you declare to be. You can access your resources in a variety of ways — in the browser, via GitHub Desktop or another desktop application, with the API, or via the command line — and each way supports different modes of authentication: username and password (or social login) with two-factor authentication, or a passkey (GitHub Free and GitHub Enterprise Cloud only); a personal access token; or an SSH key. The article then covers authenticating in your browser, with GitHub Desktop, with the API, with the command line, and GitHub's token formats.

API-specific recommendations: You can authenticate with the API in different ways (see "Authenticating to the REST API"). For personal use of the REST API, you can create a personal access token, and GitHub recommends using a fine-grained personal access token instead of a personal access token (classic). To use the API on behalf of an organization or another user, GitHub recommends a GitHub App; you can also create an OAuth token with an OAuth app, but GitHub recommends a GitHub App instead because GitHub Apps allow more control over the access and permissions the app has. In a GitHub Actions workflow, GitHub recommends authenticating with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN instead of creating a token; you can grant it permissions with the "permissions" key, and note that GITHUB_TOKEN can only access resources within the repository that contains the workflow.

Exact Docs URL cited: https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/about-authentication-to-github

JavaScript (JS) is a lightweight interpreted (or just-in-time compiled) programming language with first-class functions. While it is most well-known as the scripting language for Web pages, many non-browser environments also use it, such as Node.js, Apache CouchDB, and Adobe Acrobat.
